faq_slots.question: How often should air conditioning be serviced?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What decides it rather than a number (the trade facts servicing interval row: varies, no universal legal interval): the maker's instructions for the unit, a warranty condition that asks for a service record where the client's maker has one, and on larger commercial systems the leak checks the rules set by how much gas the system holds, which are a separate duty from a service. Why a check before the hot weather: dust on the filter and the indoor coil cuts the air crossing it, so the unit works harder on the first warm days and a slow leak shows as a unit that cannot keep up. A frequency only from [CV: visit_frequency_options] or the facts rows; never 'a yearly service is required by law'.

faq_slots.question: Why is my air conditioning blowing warm air?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Three genuinely different causes in plain words: too little air crossing the indoor coil (a filter or a coil clogged with dust), gas lost through a leak so there is less of it to carry the heat out of the room, and a control or sensor fault. Then what the local buildings or air add (a busy road loading the filters, salt air on the outdoor coil), then the fix in the order the trade facts repair stages give it: the fault found first, a leak repaired and the circuit tested before any gas goes back. A top up without finding the leak lasts weeks, never say it is a fix.

faq_slots.question: Does my air conditioning need regassing?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The refrigerant is sealed in and is not consumed, so a system short of gas has a leak somewhere (the trade facts leak found row). What the work involves from the repair stages: the leak located and repaired, the circuit tested and evacuated, then the gas put back and the repair checked again. Never regassing on its own as the answer. Sealed system work as something the trade's rules keep to engineers with the refrigerant handling certificate, as what usually applies to anyone doing it; this business's own certificate only from [CV: credentials].

faq_slots.question: When is the best time of year to have air conditioning fitted or serviced?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The reason in the system, never in the diary: a service before the hot weather finds a tired filter, a dirty coil, a slow drain or a slow leak before the unit is asked to work hard; a unit that heats as well as cools is in use through winter, so its service follows the maker's instructions rather than the season. The facts rows give no closed season and no duration for fitting a system, so say the timing of an install is decided by when the room or the building can spare it. Nothing about summer being busy or lead times stretching. No dates, no promise about the weather.

faq_slots.question: Can I clean the air conditioning filters myself?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Yes to the indoor filter, done the way the maker's leaflet for that unit says, and why it helps (the air across the coil). Then the line: the sealed circuit, the gas and the electrics are work for an engineer who holds the refrigerant handling certificate, as the trade's rule and never as this business's own certificate unless [CV: credentials] gives it. No health claim about the air.

faq_slots.question: Will the outdoor unit need planning permission?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": a unit that only cools falls outside the automatic right at a house, so a check with the council is usual; a unit that heats as well can qualify when its conditions are met; a listed home or a conservation area usually needs permission; in a flat the freeholder usually has to agree first; a business's plant has no automatic right. What the customer does only as the row gives it (apply where the conditions are not met). No volume, no count of units, no noise figure, never an Order's or an Act's name.

cards.title: Servicing that slipped a year or two
cards.brief: Schedule led: what slips when nobody services the system, from the trade facts servicing signs row: the airflow weaker each summer, the unit running longer and cooling less, a stale smell when it starts, a drip from the indoor unit. The one cause this card makes: dust building on the filter and the indoor coil, so less air crosses it, with the drain and the pressures never looked at behind it. Time of year and the reason: a check before the hot weather, because that is when the filter and the coil are asked to pass the most air and a slow leak shows as a unit that cannot keep up; never that summer is busy. What a service does, from the servicing stages: the filters and heat exchangers cleaned, the condensate run checked, the controls, a leak check where the system's gas content asks for one, the test run and the record. No interval unless the facts rows or [CV: visit_frequency_options] give one; never 'required by law every year' (the trade facts servicing interval row). By category: Air Conditioning Contractor and HVAC Contractor read it as the service itself; Repair Shop as the repairs that trace back to a missed service; Duct Cleaning as the ducts: dust at the grilles, a kitchen canopy heavy with grease, from the duct cleaning signs row.
cards.mechanism: dust building on the filter and the indoor coil, so less air crosses it

cards.title: A drip from the indoor unit
cards.brief: Problem led: a wet patch or a run mark on the wall under the indoor unit, a stain spreading on the ceiling under a cassette, water in the tray that never clears. The one cause this card makes: the drain that carries the condensate away has blocked with the dust and the film washed off a coil nobody cleaned, or was run without a fall when the unit went in, so the tray fills and spills (the trade facts servicing and split system rows). Say what the fix usually involves, from the repair stages in plain words: the drain cleared or re run, a pump where gravity cannot do it (the materials cell), the coil cleaned so it does not block again; what it leads to if left, from the skipped row: stained finishes and water near the electrics, specific and never alarming. Never that a drip proves a gas leak (the trade facts condensate row). By category: Repair Shop and HVAC Contractor read it as the fault; Air Conditioning Contractor as the drain route on a new system; Duct Cleaning as damp at a grille where moist air sits in a duct. Not weak cooling: card 1 and the symptom FAQ own that.
cards.mechanism: a condensate drain that has blocked, so the tray overflows

cards.title: Warm air, or a unit that never catches up
cards.brief: Problem led: air from the indoor unit no cooler than the room, the outdoor unit running with nothing changing indoors, ice on the pipes, a unit that trips. The one cause this card makes: gas lost through a leak, so there is less of it to carry the heat out of the room; the refrigerant is sealed in and not consumed, so a system short of it has a leak (the trade facts leak found row). Say the honest order of the work from the repair stages: the fault found, the leak located and repaired, the circuit tested and evacuated, and only then the gas put back; a top up on its own lasts weeks, never say it is a fix. Sealed system work as something the trade's rules keep to engineers with the refrigerant handling certificate, as what usually applies to anyone doing it; this business's own certificate only from [CV: credentials]. Not a filter or a coil clogged with dust: card 1 owns that; not a unit sized wrong for the room: card 4 owns that. By category: Repair Shop and HVAC Contractor read it as the fault; Air Conditioning Contractor as the joint that was never tested when the system went in (the done badly row); Duct Cleaning as a ducted system whose air cannot get through, from the ductwork signs row.
cards.mechanism: gas lost through a leak, so less heat is carried out

cards.title: A room the house can't keep cool
cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: a bedroom under the roof still warm at midnight, a home office where the afternoon sun comes through the glass, a meeting room full of people, a server cupboard whose kit trips in a hot week. What decides it: where the heat comes in (the roof, the glass, the people, the equipment) and whether anything is sized to take it out; a portable unit in the doorway does not spread cool air through the room the way a fixed system does (the trade facts installation skipped row), with no performance figure (none is verified). What the work gives them: a split sized to that room from a heat gain survey (the installation stages), the indoor unit where the air reaches the whole room, the outdoor unit where the neighbours will not hear it and an engineer can reach it; a unit too big stops and starts and leaves the room clammy, one too small runs flat out and never gets there (the sizing guidance, no percentage). By category: Air Conditioning Contractor and HVAC Contractor read it as the install; Duct Cleaning as a room that is stuffy rather than hot, where the extract barely draws (the ductwork signs row), and what a proper supply and extract gives it; Repair Shop as an old unit that never kept up because it was never sized to the room. Never a lifestyle line, never a symptom invented for it; domestic and commercial never in one sentence: [CV: customer_types] decides which leads.
cards.mechanism: the room's heat gain, and nothing sized to take it out

problem_card.title: The first hot week finds every weak spot

faq_symptom.answer_brief: The symptom and its linked local issue, answered as asked, with the cause put in the airflow, the coil, the drain or the refrigerant circuit. Say first when a sign is normal (a drip outside on a humid day, the fan running on after the unit is switched off, a smell on the first start of the year that clears in minutes) and then what is not, before anything else. Then the usual cause here in plain words, what the local buildings or air add, and what this service does about it. Never a health claim. One figure at most.

problem_card.title: Asked for its most after months idle
problem_card.brief: What shows on the first warm days after a system has sat through the cold months, from the trade facts signs row for this service. Say first what is normal (a stale smell for a minute, a drip outside, the outdoor fan running on) and then what is not (warm air, ice on the pipe, a trip, a drip indoors). The one cause this card makes: dust settling and a slow leak creeping while the system idled, now showing together. Say what gets looked at before the hot weather from confirmed practices only; otherwise what the job puts right. Not a coil icing for want of air (card 4) and not a leak left behind a top up (card 2).
problem_card.mechanism: dust settling and a slow leak creeping while the system idled

faq_slot.question: When is the best time of year for [SERVICE_LOWER], and how long does it take?
faq_slot.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing row only: the season the work suits and why, in the system (a service before the cooling season as the maker's guidance has it; nothing else in the rows has a season), then what decides how long it takes, since the rows give no duration (the units, the route, the access, whether the circuit is opened). No dates, no lead times, no promise about the weather. This is the one place the timing is written.

cards.title: A room that holds the heat
cards.brief: The customer's situation: a bedroom under the roof still warm at midnight, an office where the afternoon sun comes through the glass, a shop floor or a meeting room full of people, a server cupboard whose kit trips in a hot week, a new build or an extension that needs its ventilation (the trade facts signs rows for installation, split systems, ductwork, MVHR, server rooms and cold rooms). What decides it: where the heat or the moisture comes from (the roof, the glass, the people, the equipment, the cooking and the showers) and the building it is in (a flat, a terrace where the pipe run is harder, a listed home, a live kitchen). What the work gives them, from the stages for this service: a system sized from a heat gain survey, the indoor unit placed to reach the whole room, the outdoor unit where it is quiet and reachable, a ventilation design that supplies the living rooms and extracts the wet ones, a cold room built to its storage duty, cooling designed to the IT load with the failover written down. Homes and businesses never in one sentence: [CV: customer_types] decides which leads. Never a fault invented for it, never a lifestyle line.
cards.mechanism: where the heat comes in, and nothing sized to take it out

cards.title: Sized and sited, not just fitted
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they have had a quote by the brochure, or a cheap one, and want to know what the difference buys. What decides it: the heat gain calculation (a unit too big stops and starts and leaves the room clammy, one too small runs flat out: the sizing guidance, no percentage), the outdoor unit's position (noise to the neighbours, the air round it, service access, permission), the drain given a fall or a pump, the nitrogen test and the vacuum before any gas goes in (the split system stages; the done badly rows: joints that leak, moisture left in the circuit, a drain that leaks). For ductwork and MVHR: rigid runs where they can be, joints sealed, the flows measured and balanced (the done badly rows: unsealed joints, crushed flexible runs, terminals that miss their flow). What the work gives them: a system that does what it was bought for. One specific from the stages for this service; never a dig at another installer.
cards.mechanism: the sizing and the siting, which decide noise, airflow and running

cards.title: Which system suits the room
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they are weighing a wall mounted split against a multi split, a ducted system above the ceiling against a cassette, a unit that heats as well as cools against one that only cools, a heat recovery unit against extract fans in a new build, an integral cabinet against remote plant, close control against a split for a server room (the trade facts materials and methods cells). What decides it: how many rooms, where the units can go, whether it must heat too (a unit that only cools is never described as heating: the trade facts split system heating row), how airtight the home is for heat recovery (the MVHR operation row), the storage duty of a cold room. What the work gives them: the option that suits their building, never the one that is best in general. A named maker or product only from [CV: materials_methods]; no running cost, lifespan or energy rating claim unless the rows or the client values give it; never that air conditioning improves the home's energy rating (the trade facts EPC row).
cards.mechanism: the room, the building and its use deciding the kind of system

cards.title: What it will ask of you once it's in
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they want to know what they are taking on once the system is in. What decides it: the indoor filter they can clean themselves following the maker's instructions; a service at the interval the maker's instructions and any warranty condition set (that condition from the client's maker's terms only, never generalised: the trade facts warranty row); on a business's system the leak checks and records the rules ask for by the gas held, and the energy inspection on larger systems, said as duties banded by size with no figure; a kitchen canopy cleaned to a risk based band; a cold room's alarms and door seals; the handover information that comes with a ventilation system (the ventilation handover row). What the work gives them: an honest picture of what it saves them and what it does not. A servicing plan or a contract only where the services list has one; no response time; no health claim.
cards.mechanism: what the system needs to keep doing its job

problem_card.title: Getting it in before it's needed
problem_card.brief: The customer's situation: they want it in before the hot weather, or want to know when it should be fitted. What decides it: the facts rows give no closed season for fitting, so the timing is set by the building: a room not yet relying on it, a shutdown window on a working site, a stock move planned for a cold room, a live server room changed over without losing cooling (the trade facts timing cells for installation, commercial systems, server rooms and cold rooms). What the work gives them: a system in and commissioned while the building can spare it. No dates, nothing about summer being busy or lead times stretching, no promise about the weather.
problem_card.mechanism: a system fitted while the building can spare it

faq_slot.question: When is the best time of year for [SERVICE_LOWER], and how long does it take?
faq_slot.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing row only: the rows give no season and no duration for fitting a system, so say what sets the timing (when the room or the building can spare it, a shutdown window, a stock move) and what decides how long it takes (the units, the route, the access). No dates, no lead times, no promise about the weather. This is the one place the timing is written.

cards.title: Rooms under the roof that hold the heat
cards.brief: Loft rooms, top floor flats and rooms behind big glass that stay warm into the night. The one cause this card makes: the town's housing, which the town profile gives (loft conversions, top floor flats, new build estates with their mechanical ventilation, glass fronted offices). Say what the housing means for the work in plain words: where a unit can go in a loft room, what a top floor flat needs agreed before anything is fitted, what a new estate's ventilation unit needs looking after; never that the town's homes are overheating or unhealthy (the pack's local detail rule). Not the heat gain of one room: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: the town's housing: loft rooms and top floors the sun gets into

cards.title: Nowhere obvious for the outdoor unit
cards.brief: Period terraces where the pipe run is long and the back wall is the only wall, flats where the unit must go on a balcony or the roof, streets where a unit on the front would be seen from the road. The one cause this card makes: buildings that limit where the outdoor unit can sit, from the town profile (the terraces, the flats, the conservation areas, only where the profile confirms them). What usually applies, with "usually" and never an Order's name: a flat's freeholder has to agree first; in a conservation area or at a listed home the unit's position is settled with the council before it is fitted. Say what it means for the route and the noise to the neighbours. Not the sizing: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: buildings that limit where the outdoor unit can sit

cards.title: Salt, traffic and the outdoor coil
cards.brief: Outdoor units that corrode early near the sea, filters that clog early on a main road, units whose noise carries on a dense street. The one cause this card makes: the town's air loading the coils and the filters, from the town profile only (the coast, the busy roads, the tight streets). Every anchor changes the work: salt on the outdoor coil means it is looked at more often and the fins kept clean; a main road means the filters are checked sooner; a tight street means the outdoor unit's position is chosen for the neighbours. Not the servicing schedule itself: the servicing page owns that. Never a local temperature record.
cards.mechanism: the town's air loading the coils and the filters

cards.title: Kitchens, shops and server rooms on the high street
cards.brief: Restaurant streets whose canopies fill with grease as the hours run, food shops with cold rooms holding stock, offices and business parks with a server room that must not stop. The one cause this card makes: the town's commercial mix and what each building asks of its system, from the town profile only. Say what each means for the work (the canopy cleaned to a risk based band, the cold room's temperature held and alarmed, the server room's cooling changed over without losing it), as what the work meets and never as a judgement on anyone's system. Homes and businesses never in one sentence; this card leads commercial only where [CV: customer_types] says so.
cards.mechanism: the town's commercial mix and what each building asks of its system

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [WORK] in [TOWN]

cards.title: Where the outdoor unit can go
cards.brief: A terrace with no side access, a flat where the unit goes on a balcony or the roof, a wall only reached from height: the outdoor unit's position and the access to it move the price (the trade facts price rows). From the town profile where it gives the housing. No figure.

cards.title: Long runs through older houses
cards.brief: Period houses where the pipe and drain route is long or has to be hidden, and a pump where the drain cannot fall (the price rows). From the profile where it gives the housing era. Say why a long or concealed route costs more time.

cards.title: Permissions and the neighbours
cards.brief: Where the town has conservation areas, listed homes or many flats, the planning or noise work and the freeholder's agreement before a unit is fitted add time. "Usually", never the Order's or the area's official name. From the dossier rules only.

cards.title: Working round a business's hours
cards.brief: Commercial premises where the changeover waits for a shutdown window, a live room kept cool while the plant is swapped, stock moved before a cold room is touched (the price rows). Only where the profile gives the commercial mix; work outside opening hours only from the confirmed practices. No figure.

faq_slots.question: How much does [WORK_LOWER] cost in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Prices only from [CV: price_list]; otherwise the things that push the price up in a town like this (where the outdoor unit can go, the route, permissions) and how the quote is given, from [CV: quote_method] only.

faq_slots.question: How soon can you get to [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: start_time] and [CV: response_time] only. The town is in the area covered; nothing about distance unless [CV: travel_distance] is set.

faq_slots.question: Do you cover [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Yes: the town and the villages around it (code lists them; name none). How the business reaches it from its base only from the client values. Link one page in this town.

faq_slots.question: Do you guarantee your work in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Start with yes, then the terms from [CV: guarantee_years] and [CV: guarantee_scope]. A maker's warranty only from [CV: manufacturer_warranty]. Described, never promised.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if something isn't right after the job?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: What happens when I ask for a quote in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] and the confirmed practices only: what the customer sends (which rooms, the unit's label, photos), what the business looks at (the room's heat, the route, the power, the drain), what comes back. No timescale unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slots.question: Is there a best time of year for [WORK_LOWER] work in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The reason in the system, from the trade facts timing cells: a service before the hot weather, because the filter, the coil and the drain are then asked to do their most and a slow leak shows as a unit that cannot keep up; fitting a system has no closed season in the rows. Where the town profile gives the exposure (salt air on the coast, a main road), say what it does to how often the outdoor coil and the filters are looked at. Nothing about summer being busy or lead times. No dates, no promise about the weather.
